newsitem.title: USA: TV rating negotiations deadlocked over moratorium.
newsitem.headline: TV rating negotiations deadlocked over moratorium.

text.p: Negotiators for the television industry and advocacy groups are deadlocked over a key issue in talks to revamp the industry's programme-rating system, sources close to the talks said Friday.
The sticking point is the length of a proposed moratorium during which the groups would refrain from pushing for congressionally mandated changes to the new ratings.
Industry executives want a three-year moratorium while the groups -- which include the Children's Defence Fund, the Centre for Media Education, the National PTA, and others -- want an 18-month truce.
The executives have agreed tentatively to alter their existing age-based ratings to include the letters "V," "S," and "L" to designate violence, sexual content and coarse language.

The letters would be added to the "TV-PG," "TV-14" and "TV-M" ratings. TV-PG refers to parental guidance suggested; TV-14 to parents of children under 14 strongly cautioned; and TV-M to mature audiences only.
Senate lawmakers, meanwhile, have refrained for now from acting on legislation that would require changes in the hopes that the two sides can reach a voluntary agreement.
A bill pushed by Sen. Dan Coats, an Indiana Republican, would pull the broadcast license of a TV station that does not divulge content information about its shows.

Representative W.J. (Billy) Tauzin, R-La., has drafted a letter in the House that pledges lawmakers to refrain from pushing for legislative fixes for the foreseeable future if the TV industry and the advocacy groups can reach agreement.

Ken Johnson, Tauzin's spokesman, said House Speaker Newt Gingrich has agreed in principle with the letter. House Commerce Committee Chairman Thomas Bliley, R-Va., is reviewing the document, said Johnson.
